name: Qualifier Density Pattern
description: Analyzes the frequency of qualifier words (e.g., 'very', 'quite', 'somewhat', 'almost', 'probably', 'typically', 'generally') used to modify adjectives or verbs. Large Language Models, heavily conditioned by RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) to remain neutral, safe, and academically accommodating, suffer from a chronic overuse of qualifiers. They habitually use these words to soften claims or hedge statements, resulting in a significantly higher density of mitigating language compared to confident human writing.
mechanism: The algorithm parses the text using a part-of-speech (POS) tagger to identify adverbs, specific adjectives, and auxiliary verb phrases acting as qualifiers. It calculates the 'Qualifier/Word Ratio' and cross-references it against the 'Absolute Claim Index' (the frequency of definitive statements). AI-generated texts consistently exhibit an unnaturally high qualifier density (a pathological need to say 'it is *generally* considered' or 'this *can* be seen as *somewhat* beneficial') because definitive statements carry a higher mathematical penalty during safety fine-tuning. The system flags texts where the density of these softening words mathematically eclipses natural human rhetorical limits.
useCase: Highly effective for auditing persuasive essays, journalism, opinion pieces, and marketing copy where human writers typically employ strong, unmitigated assertions, whereas AI introduces artificial hesitation.
strengths:
• Directly attacks the safety-alignment conditioning (RLHF) of modern LLMs, which is almost impossible for an AI to turn off completely without complex, aggressive prompting.
• Extremely robust across different LLM architectures (GPT, Claude, Gemini), as they all share similar safety-training paradigms.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives in scientific writing, legal disclaimers, or academic literature reviews, where extensive qualification and hedging are the required professional standard.
• Short texts (<100 words) may not contain enough data points to establish a reliable density baseline.
parameters:
Analysis: Lexical Qualifier Extraction and Hedging Detection
Metric: Frequency of Mitigating Modifiers per 100 Words
Output: 0-100 Qualifier Overload (Artificial Hesitation) Score
accuracy: High — 80-88% accuracy on persuasive and opinion texts. Accuracy drops in formal scientific contexts where hedging is natural.

references.title: Uchendu, A. et al. (2020). Authorship Attribution for Neural Text Generation. EMNLP.
Guo, B. et al. (2023). How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? Comparison Corpus, Evaluation, and Detection. NeurIPS.
